g.text: Tiling quantizes space - which is what converts a compute problem into a static-asset problem
An on-demand render is keyed by an arbitrary bounding box, so no two users request the same one, the cache hit rate is ~zero, and EVERY request reaches the origin.
Why tile at all
-> an arbitrary key nobody else will ever request
tiled: GET /{z}/{x}/{y}.mvt
-> a key EVERY client in that area computes identically
The naive alternative - take vector road data, draw it at the requested zoom,
return an image - is flexible and wrong for two reasons that compound.
It puts COMPUTE IN FRONT OF IMMUTABLE DATA: the map of San Francisco does not
change between requests, so rendering it per request recomputes an identical
answer millions of times a day.
And it DESTROYS CACHEABILITY, which is the fatal one. At 1 billion DAU, a design
where every request reaches the origin is not a scaling problem you can buy your
way out of.
Tiling fixes both by quantizing space into a fixed grid: there are only so many tiles, every client asking about the same area
asks for the SAME tile, and the answer never changes. Static assets at global scale is a solved problem with a name.
Each level up quadruples the count and doubles the linear resolution
zoom 0
1 tile (1x1) the whole world in 256x256 pixels
zoom 1
4 tiles (2x2)
zoom 2
16 tiles (4x4)
zoom 21
4.4 TRILLION tiles ~building-level detail
n = 2^z
x = floor( n * (lng + 180) / 360 )
y = floor( n * (1 - ln(tan(lat) + sec(lat)) / pi) / 2 )
Ugly, deterministic, and CHEAP ENOUGH TO RUN ON THE CLIENT - which is the property
that matters, because it removes a round trip from the most frequent operation in
the product.
What a viewport actually costs: a 1080x1920 phone screen at 256-pixel tiles needs
about 5 x 8 = 40 TILES, and fewer in practice with device pixel ratios and
512-pixel variants. So a full map view is a few dozen small PARALLEL requests,
all independently cacheable - and a partially-loaded map still renders usefully.
That graceful degradation comes free from tiles being independent, and it is why
a map on a poor connection fills in progressively rather than blocking.
The client computes the URL - and pays for it with a near-permanent convention
Panning and zooming are continuous gestures generating tile requests many times per second. An intermediate 'resolve my tiles'
call would add a round trip to every gesture - and a round trip to a SERVER, whereas the tile fetches themselves go to a nearby
CDN edge. You would be adding the slowest hop in the system to the most frequent operation in the product.
so (z,x,y) addressing, Web Mercator and 256-pixel tiles are effectively FROZEN AT LAUNCH
GET /v1/tiles/resolve?lat=..&lng=..&zoom=.. -> { urls: [...] }
Old app versions keep computing old URLs for years and you cannot force an upgrade. The standard hedge is to ALSO offer a
server-side resolution API that clients may opt into: newer clients get flexibility (the server could switch schemes, serve a
different projection, or A/B test tile sizes) at the cost of one extra call. Not a solution so much as an escape hatch - worth
having, and worth being honest that the default path is the frozen one.
Vector versus raster - and the second benefit is bigger than the bandwidth one
raster (PNG / JPEG)
VECTOR (MVT / protobuf)
contents
pixels
paths, polygons, labels, attributes
typical size
who renders
the server, in advance
the CLIENT, at display time
restyle (dark mode, satellite)
a new tile set per style
the same tiles, different style rules
intermediate zoom
blurry upscale
smooth - geometry scales cleanly
label rotation / localization
baked in
client-side: per-language labels from one tile
client CPU / battery
minimal
HIGHER
client complexity
draw an image
a rendering engine
Vector wins on the requirement that matters most - 'data and battery frugality' - because vector tiles are 5-10x SMALLER, the
single largest bandwidth saving available in the product.
But the easily-overlooked benefit is arguably bigger: ONE TILE SET SERVES EVERY STYLE AND EVERY LANGUAGE. Dark mode, satellite
overlay, transit emphasis, high-contrast accessibility and 80 languages of labels are all CLIENT-SIDE STYLE RULES applied to
the same geometry. Under raster tiling, each of those would be a separate 60 PB TILE SET. So vector tiles do not just save
bandwidth - they avoid multiplying the largest dataset in the system by the number of visual variants, which is what makes
those variants economically possible at all.
The genuine cost is client CPU, and it partially fights the requirement it serves: you save RADIO energy and spend GPU energy.
On modern hardware the radio dominates so the trade is clearly favourable - but it is a real trade rather than a free win, and
it means very old devices get a worse experience.
Three things make 60 PB tractable, and the first matters most
1 deduplicate uniform tiles
(21, 300001, 400000) -+-> hash 3f8a... -> ONE stored object
At zoom 21 a tile covering open Pacific contains NOTHING - and so do the billions
around it. They are byte-identical, so tiles are content-addressed: hash the
bytes, store one copy per distinct hash, map (z,x,y) -> hash. It also improves
the CDN, because a single hot ocean tile is cached once per edge instead of being
billions of distinct COLD objects.
2 don't precompute every level everywhere
Zoom 21 is only meaningful where there is detail to show. Dense cities are generated to 21; open ocean stops at maybe zoom 8,
because there is nothing further to reveal. Requests below the generated depth upscale the deepest available tile -
imperceptible when the content is featureless. So the tile set is DEEP WHERE INFORMATION DENSITY IS HIGH AND SHALLOW
ELSEWHERE, which is the same density-adaptive principle a quadtree applies to point data, here applied to storage depth.
3 let the CDN do the work
client -> CDN edge (nearest PoP)
HIT (~99%) -> served locally, origin never involved
MISS ( ~1%) -> fetch from object-storage origin, cache, serve
The ~99% hit rate holds because tile requests are extremely concentrated - cities,
motorways, tourist destinations - and immutability lets an edge cache a tile
INDEFINITELY with Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable.
Two CDN behaviours are load-bearing. REQUEST COLLAPSING turns concurrent edge
misses for the same key into ONE origin fetch - without it, a suddenly-popular
location delivers thousands of identical origin requests at once, a thundering
herd on a per-object basis. And PREFETCHING ADJACENT TILES buys the perception of
an instantly-responsive map at the cost of bandwidth for tiles that may go
unused, which on a metered connection is a genuine trade - so it is usually tuned
by connection type.
Roads change - and purging trillions of cached objects is not a realistic operation
/v41/{z}/{x}/{y}.mvt <- current
/v42/{z}/{x}/{y}.mvt <- published alongside; nothing invalidated
GET /v1/map/version -> { 'tiles_version': 42 } <- the ONE thing clients poll
You would have to enumerate affected tiles, issue purges to every PoP, and wait
for eventual propagation with no reliable completion signal. So updates are
VERSIONED, NOT PURGED.
Publishing v42 invalidates nothing. Clients discover it through one tiny version
endpoint (itself cached with a short TTL) and start requesting the new prefix.
Old tiles stay valid for clients that have not checked yet, so THERE IS NO MOMENT
OF INCONSISTENCY - a client is always on exactly one coherent version.
And rollback is a POINTER CHANGE: set the version endpoint back to 41. Nothing needs re-uploading or re-warming, because v41 is
still cached everywhere. Compare purge-based invalidation, where a bad publish means re-purging and then re-warming trillions
of objects from a cold origin.
The costs are honest ones. Storage multiplies with retained versions - mitigated by content-addressed dedup, since v41 and v42
share every unchanged tile, so a new version costs only the tiles that actually changed. And v42 STARTS COLD at the edges, so
a publish causes a temporary origin load spike as popular tiles are re-fetched; staging the version endpoint's rollout by
region turns that spike into a ramp.
